newsitem.title: FRANCE: French insurer AGF studies Holocaust suit.
newsitem.headline: French insurer AGF studies Holocaust suit.

text.p: French insurer Assurances Generales de France (AGF) said on Thursday it would try to help the families of Jews who may have bought insurance policies from it before or during World War Two and were later sent to Nazi death camps.
But since all of its records from the war era had long ago been destroyed, it would need some evidence of the existence of such policies before it could do anything, a company spokesman said.
"We have no intention of denying anything if there is something due to somebody," AGF spokesman Francois Vikar told Reuters.
"If we just get even one page from people saying they put money into a policy, then we can look into it," Vikar said.

He was responding to a lawsuit filed in New York this week by a group of Holocaust victims and their families, alleging that AGF and six other European insurance firms withheld, concealed or converted the cash value and proceeds of policies sold to the victims prior to 1946.
The lawsuit, filed in Manhattan federal court, estimates that more than 10,000 people stood to benefit from the suit. It seeks billions of dollars in damages, to be determined at trial.
Vikar said the group filing the initial suit, which seeks class-action status under U.S. law, consisted of just nine individuals.
Of those, just one, a woman from Brooklyn, had alleged that a relative bought a policy from Phoenix Insurance, a corporate predecessor of AGF, he said.
He said the company had just received a copy of the suit and did not yet know what evidence the woman had of her relative's insurance policy.

The other firms named in the suit were Assicurazioni Generali S.p.A. of Trieste, Italy; Wiener Allianz Verischerungs Aktiengesellschaft of Vienna; Riunione Adriatica Di Sicurta S.p.A. of Milan; Allianz Group of Munich; Der Anker Allgemeine Versicherungs AG of Vienna, and Bavarian Reinsurance Co of Munich.
